changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment: The registry's sequence, on the vendors that have sequences — created in the same breath as its table, the lesson email-connector's 1.0.0-43 paid for and its 1.0.0-47/49 had to repeat.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
The CalDAV server registry: one row per server an administrator declared, holding only what any authenticated user may see. Credentials are deliberately absent — per-user secrets stay in the per-user settings storage — so a read of this table can never leak one.
PROVIDER_NAME is the bridge to agenda's REMOTE_PROVIDER by name: agenda.caldavCalendar for the seed row (migrated from the legacy exo.agenda.caldav.connector.url property), agenda.caldavCalendar.<id> for the rows declared afterwards. System-derived, never typed by anyone, and unique — the separate index changeset below.
The unique index does NOT live in this changeset, on purpose: modifySql is changeset-scoped, so the mysql ENGINE/CHARSET append below would also be glued onto a CREATE INDEX sharing the changeset, which MySQL rejects with error 1064 — and a failed changeset here takes the whole platform down through Liquibase → entityManagerFactory → the Kernel/Spring bridge. email-connector's 1.0.0-46/50 is the precedent, paid for on an acceptance server.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment: CALDAV_SERVER's unique index on PROVIDER_NAME, in its own changeset with NO modifySql — the separation the createTable comment above explains. Uniqueness is what makes the provider name a safe join key to agenda's REMOTE_PROVIDER: two rows sharing one provider name would silently steer two server URLs through a single enabled-switch.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment: The visual identity of a registered server, exactly as email-connector carries it: ICON holds a font-icon class chosen from the picker, IMAGE_FILE_ID an uploaded image stored through FileService — the row renders the image when both exist. A NEW changeset with addColumn and deliberately NO modifySql: modifySql is changeset-scoped and its ENGINE/CHARSET append is only valid on CREATE TABLE — appending it to an ALTER TABLE is the same class of mistake as appending it to CREATE INDEX, the one 1.0.0-2's comment recounts.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment: The calendar-pair sequence, created in the same breath as its table for the reason 1.0.0-0 records.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
One row per binding between an eXo calendar and a remote collection, for one user on one declared server. Carries the identity of the pair and the state of their last exchange — never calendar content.
LOCAL_CALENDAR_SYNC_UID is agenda's immutable per-calendar anchor, not the calendar's technical id: an id is a database identity a restore or a migration may renumber, while the sync uid is minted once and never changes. It is null for the MIRROR pair alone, which has no local calendar.
REMOTE_HREF is stored canonical — percent-decoded, no trailing slash — so that two spellings of one collection compare equal. A binding that compared raw hrefs would lose its pair the first time a server answered a differently-escaped one.
No unique constraint on REMOTE_HREF: at NVARCHAR(1000) it exceeds MySQL's index key length under utf8mb4 (4 bytes per character against a 3072-byte limit). Uniqueness is carried by the calendar anchor instead, in 1.0.0-6.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
One pair per local calendar, per server, per user. Own changeset with no modifySql, per 1.0.0-2.
Standard SQL leaves rows with a NULL anchor outside this constraint, so it does not by itself stop a second MIRROR pair — that one is guarded in the service, which is also where the decision to create it is made. The index is here for the case the database can actually enforce, and for the lookup the engine performs on every sync.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment: The background sweep selects pairs by state — what is active and due, what is paused, what needs attention — across every user at once. Without this index that is a full scan of the table on every run.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment: The object-mapping sequence, with its table, per 1.0.0-0.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
One row per calendar object inside a pair: the eXo event, the iCalendar UID both sides agree on, where it sits remotely, the server's ETag and a hash of what eXo last pushed.
These four columns are what let the engine verify and detect deletions without keeping a second copy of the calendar. They answer the only three questions it asks — is our copy still there, has anyone else changed it, and would what we are about to push differ from what is already stored.
LOCAL_EVENT_ID is nullable: an object can exist remotely before it has been materialised locally.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
One object row per iCalendar UID within a pair. This is the constraint that makes the backfill idempotent by construction rather than by convention: re-running it cannot produce a second row for an event that already has one.
BIGINT plus NVARCHAR(250) is 1008 bytes under utf8mb4, inside MySQL's 3072-byte index key limit — which is why the UID rather than the href carries uniqueness here too.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment: Objects belong to their pair: unbinding a calendar must not leave object rows pointing at a pair that no longer exists. Own changeset, no modifySql, for the reason 1.0.0-3 records about ALTER TABLE.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
PUSHED_HASH goes. It held a digest of the calendar object eXo had pushed, so that a later pass could tell "the server changed this" from "this is exactly what we wrote" - and no such digest can be captured. A CalDAV server is entitled to re-serialise the document it is given; BlueMind does, and it finishes doing so after the write returns, without moving the ETag, so the digest was wrong however it was taken. EXO-89716 replaces the check with a comparison against the object eXo would render for the event now, which needs nothing stored at all.
Dropped rather than left dead: a column nobody writes is a column the next reader has to work out the status of. 1.0.0-9, which created it, is not touched - a changeset's identity is its file, id and author, and every database that has already run it must go on agreeing that it ran.
The rollback is written out because dropColumn has no automatic one, and it restores the column and not its contents: the digests are gone, and a revert would find every row blank. That was already the value the previous code treated as "written before the hash was recorded, judge nothing".

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
Whether eXo writes its Accept / Decline / Tentative links into the description of the meeting copies pushed to this server (EXO-89757).
Per server rather than global: one deployment can connect BlueMind and Stalwart at once and want different answers for each, because whether a calendar client offers its own RSVP control is a property of the clients used against that server and of nothing else.
DEFAULT TRUE and NOT NULL, so every row that already exists keeps writing the links it writes today - the setting ships behaviour-neutral. The asymmetry is deliberate: redundant links are a mild annoyance, missing links leave a user unable to answer at all.
addColumn with deliberately NO modifySql, for the reason 1.0.0-3 records and 1.0.0-2 recounts: the ENGINE/CHARSET append is only valid on CREATE TABLE, and gluing it onto an ALTER TABLE is the MySQL-1064 failure that takes the whole platform down through Liquibase.
No rollback is written because addColumn has an automatic one - unlike the dropColumn above, which needed its own.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
The pending-push sequence, on the vendors that have sequences - created in the same breath as its table, the lesson 1.0.0-0 records.
Numbered from 20 rather than from 14 on purpose: 1.0.0-13 is already applied on the rig and the ids in between are being taken concurrently by another delivery. A gap in the numbering costs nothing; two changesets shipping the same id costs a database that disagrees with itself about which one it ran.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
One row per calendar copy eXo owes a write to and has not managed to make (EXO-89773).
Until this existed, a push that failed left nothing behind. The log said the verification pass would retry; it never could. That pass compares the version the server publishes against the version eXo recorded, and an edit that never reached the server does not move the server's version - so the copy was judged untouched before anything was fetched, and stayed wrong for ever. A failed removal had no safety net at all: a destroyed event renders to nothing, and the pass deliberately concludes nothing from an empty render.
A table rather than two columns on CALDAV_OBJECT_SYNC, for two reasons. The mapping row has several writers and every one of them saves it whole, so a marker set between one of their reads and its save would be erased by it, silently. And this table is EMPTY once everything has landed, so the retry pass is one index lookup answering no rows - where a column on the mapping table would have made every sweep read every copy a user holds to discover that none of them is owed anything. That cost is exactly the churn EXO-89716 and EXO-89756 removed.
LOCAL_EVENT_ID is nullable because a removal has no event left to render: its meeting was destroyed, and ICS_UID is the only identity the object can still be addressed by.
ATTEMPTS bounds how hard eXo argues with a server that keeps refusing. NOT NULL with a default of zero, so a row written by a client that does not name the column still counts from the start.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment: One obligation per copy. This is what makes recording one idempotent by construction rather than by convention: a meeting edited five times in a minute owes its copy one write, not five, and the constraint says so rather than the code promising it.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
The retry is driven one account at a time, and on a converged account it must find nothing without reading anything. That is this index: an account with no backlog costs one lookup that answers no rows.
ATTEMPTS is the second column because the pass asks for the obligations still worth attempting - the abandoned ones are left where they are, as the only record that eXo gave up on them.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
An obligation belongs to the copy it is owed to: a mapping row that goes takes what was owed to it with it, because a write owed to a copy nothing points at any more would be retried against an identifier that no longer resolves.
Own changeset, no modifySql, for the reason 1.0.0-3 records about ALTER TABLE.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
The property-name patterns a server is excused for ADDING to the copies it stores - the per-server replacement for the global exo.agenda.caldav.mirror.ignoredProperties (EXO-89771).
NULLABLE, with NO default, and that is the whole upgrade story. NULL means "this row has never been asked", and the deployment-wide property goes on deciding for it, so an upgrade changes nothing anywhere. An empty string is an administrator's own answer of "excuse nothing", which must NOT fall back to the global list or unticking the last box would be a no-op. A NOT NULL DEFAULT '' would have collapsed the two and silenced the global lever on every existing deployment the moment this shipped.
Its own changeset, separate from the sibling below: a changeset's identity is permanent, and the two lists are two decisions with different lifetimes - one of them may well outlive the other.
addColumn with deliberately NO modifySql, for the reason 1.0.0-3 records: the ENGINE/CHARSET append is only valid on CREATE TABLE, and gluing it onto an ALTER TABLE is the MySQL-1064 failure that takes the whole platform down through Liquibase. No rollback is written because addColumn has an automatic one.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
The property-name patterns a server is excused for NOT KEEPING faithfully - the per-server replacement for exo.agenda.caldav.mirror.droppedProperties (EXO-89771). BlueMind keeps no CONFERENCE, and one catalogue entry - the invitation text - additionally excuses a value the server rewrites.
Same NULLABLE, no-default rule as 1.0.0-14 above, for the same reason, and the same absence of modifySql.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
What each server has actually been seen doing, as a rolling DIRECTION:PROPERTY=COUNT summary (EXO-89771). This is what the drawer offers to excuse: the administrator ticks from evidence the sweep gathered rather than from a log line they had to find and a property name they had to type correctly.
A column rather than a table, deliberately. It must survive a restart - an empty drawer after one is an empty drawer exactly when somebody is investigating - and it must stay cheap: one bounded row per server, never one row per copy per divergence. It is also read with the registration the drawer already fetches, so it costs no extra query.
Derived data, and separable on purpose: this is the one of the three columns that could be dropped later without touching the two lists an administrator's decisions live in, which is why it does not share their changesets.
Nullable, no default: a server nothing has ever been observed on carries nothing, and an empty summary and no summary mean the same thing here. Same absence of modifySql as its two siblings.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
What eXo LEAVES OUT of the copies it writes to this server (EXO-89775).
Its own column, and that separation is the point. IGNORED_PROPERTIES and DROPPED_PROPERTIES say what eXo tolerates in a copy; this one says what eXo writes into somebody's calendar. Folding a payload decision into a tolerance list would give one column two meanings, and whoever reads the row next - an administrator in the drawer, or a developer in a database client - could not tell which decision they were looking at.
It holds CASES rather than property names: SOLO-ORGANIZER, the organizer of an event with no other participants. BlueMind stores neither ORGANIZER nor ATTENDEE for such an event, so eXo wrote one, read back a copy without it, and rewrote the copy on every sweep for ever. Naming a case rather than a property is also what keeps it out of the comparison: those lists only accept a property IcsWriter emits, so no value here can make a missing organizer on an ordinary meeting stop being reported.
Nullable, no default, and nothing global behind it: unlike its two siblings there is no deployment-wide property to fall back to, so an empty value and no value both mean "eXo writes everything it writes". Same absence of modifySql, and addColumn's automatic rollback.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
Where the meeting copies pushed to this server are written (EXO-89760): DEDICATED_CALENDAR - a calendar of eXo's own, the behaviour every deployment has today - MAIN_CALENDAR, the calendar the account itself calls its default, or USER_CHOICE, which writes nothing until the user has named one.
NOT NULL with DEFAULT 'DEDICATED_CALENDAR', and the DEFAULT is the whole upgrade story - it is the same DDL clause that backfills every row an existing deployment already holds, so every server declared before this setting existed goes on writing copies exactly where it writes them today. Unlike the three excusal columns above there is no deployment-wide property standing behind this one, so a NULL would say nothing an empty value does not; collapsing them costs nothing here and saves every reader a null check on a value that always has an answer.
A name rather than a number. A numeric ordinal is unreadable in a database client and, worse, silently re-points every stored row the day somebody inserts a value into the middle of the enum.
NVARCHAR(32) leaves room for a fourth kind without a second ALTER on a table every account resolution reads.
addColumn with deliberately NO modifySql, for the reason 1.0.0-3 records: the ENGINE/CHARSET append is only valid on CREATE TABLE, and gluing it onto an ALTER TABLE is the MySQL-1064 failure that takes the whole platform down through Liquibase. No rollback is written because addColumn has an automatic one.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
When a setting of this registration that governs the COPIES last changed (EXO-89759).
The problem it answers: the mirror only ever converges towards what eXo would render now when something moves the remote ETag, so an administrator could change a setting that alters what eXo writes and nothing would happen to the copies already on the server, for ever. This column is one half of the pair that makes such a change reach them - the other is COPY_SETTINGS_APPLIED on CALDAV_CALENDAR_SYNC, added next.
NULLABLE WITH NO DEFAULT, and that is the whole upgrade story. Null means "nothing to apply": every row an existing deployment already holds starts unstamped, so no mirror finds itself behind and no full comparison is ever owed until an administrator actually changes one of the settings concerned. A DEFAULT of the current timestamp added in an edit would, on the first sweep after an upgrade, make every connected account in the deployment fetch and compare every copy it holds at once.
Deliberately NOT numbered after 1.0.0-13: the ids up to 1.0.0-17 and from 1.0.0-20 to 1.0.0-24 are claimed by changes in flight on other branches, and a changeset's identity is its file, its id and its author for every database that has already run it. Starting at 40 leaves them room to land without either side having to renumber - which is the one repair that does not exist.
addColumn with deliberately NO modifySql, for the reason 1.0.0-3 records and 1.0.0-13 recounts: the ENGINE/CHARSET append is only valid on CREATE TABLE, and gluing it onto an ALTER TABLE is the MySQL-1064 failure that takes the whole platform down through Liquibase.
No rollback is written because addColumn has an automatic one.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
The value of the server's COPY_SETTINGS_UPDATED that this pair has already carried through one full comparison of its copies (EXO-89759).
Older than the server's stamp - null included - means the next verification pass owes the copies already on the server one round that compares their content instead of trusting an unchanged ETag. Equal means there is nothing to apply, which is the state a converged pair sits in and the reason the ordinary pass keeps costing one collection listing and nothing else.
It holds the server's value rather than the moment the round ran, on purpose: a setting changed while a round is walking the pages must not be swallowed by a stamp that happens to be later than it.
NULLABLE WITH NO DEFAULT, same reasoning as 1.0.0-40 above: an unstamped pair against an unstamped server is "nothing to apply", which is where every upgraded deployment starts. It is also what makes the round resumable - a crash mid-round never reaches the stamp, so the next sweep re-runs a comparison that rewrites nothing already converged.
addColumn with no modifySql, and no rollback written, for the reasons 1.0.0-40 gives.

changeSet.author: caldav
changeSet.comment:
Which ConnectorCredentialsProvider this server uses ("personal", "bluemind-sudo"...) - the admin-facing counterpart of the shared credentials contract (commons-exo). Not PROVIDER_NAME above, which names the remote server product rather than how credentials are obtained for it. Defaulted to "personal" so every server declared before this field existed keeps working exactly as it does today, with no administrator action required.
Numbered after the last changeset the branch carries, not where it was written: a changeset's identity is its file, id and author, so an id another changeset already used on any database would be read as "already ran" and this column would never be created.
